# Syphilis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Infectious diseases > Sexually transmitted diseases > Syphilis*

[Original Article Link](/library/sk0t6T)

---

## Summary

Syphilis is a predominantly sexually transmitted bacterial infection caused by the <u>spirochete</u> <u>Treponema pallidum</u>. The disease presentation consists of four distinct, successive clinical stages (primary, secondary, latent, and tertiary) if left untreated. <u>Primary syphilis</u> manifests with a painless <u>chancre</u> (primary lesion), typically on the genitals. <u>Secondary syphilis</u> is characterized by a polymorphic, <u>maculopapular rash</u> that appears on the palms and soles. The first two stages are followed by an asymptomatic phase (<u>latent syphilis</u>), which may last indefinitely or progress to <u>tertiary syphilis</u>. During the tertiary stage, characteristic <u>granulomas</u> (<u>gumma</u>) may appear, which can cause irreversible organ damage, particularly in the <u>cardiovascular system</u> (e.g., syphilitic <u>aortic aneurysm</u>). <u>Neurosyphilis</u>, <u>ocular syphilis</u>, and <u>otosyphilis</u> are serious manifestations that can occur at any stage of infection. Treponemal or nontreponemal <u>serological studies</u> are used for screening, and the diagnosis is typically made based on clinical assessment and the interpretation of syphilis <u>serologies</u>. Alternatively, the diagnosis can be made using studies that directly detect <u>T. pallidum</u> (e.g., <u>darkfield microscopy</u>, <u>PCR</u>) if a specimen of infected tissue is obtainable. First-line <u>treatment for syphilis</u> is <u>penicillin G</u>; <u>allergen</u> sensitization should be initiated in patients with a <u>penicillin</u> <u>allergy</u>. <u>Prevention of syphilis</u> includes providing <u>counseling on safe sex practices</u> to all individuals and offering <u>syphilis screening</u> to individuals with indications.




![Syphilis fact sheet](media/op0xzs9saex8qwkg8g6nunoa.jpg)

Syphilis fact sheet

## Epidemiology

* Sex: <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u> (8:1)

* <u>Incidence</u>: 13.5/100,000 per year in the US

* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 25–29 years





References:[[1]](/library/KebU-s)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* <u>Pathogen</u>: <u>Treponema pallidum</u>: gram-negative, spiral-shaped bacteria belonging to the <u>spirochete</u> family

* Transmission  [[2]](/library/U30b3f)[[3]](/library/gTYFJo)

* Sexual contact (via small mucocutaneous lesions)

* Vertical

* <u>Blood transfusion</u> or organ donations (rare)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Treponema</u> bacteria (particularly during stages I and II) are highly contagious.

---

## Clinical features

See “Subtypes and variants” for details on <u>neurosyphilis</u>, <u>ocular syphilis</u>, and <u>otosyphilis</u>, which can occur at any stage of infection.




### <u>Incubation period</u> [[4]](/library/FkXgpy)




* 10–90 days

* On average 21 days





### Primary syphilis




* Localized disease

* 90–95%: genital <u>primary syphilis</u>

* 5–10%: extragenital <u>primary syphilis</u> (most commonly, the <u>oral cavity</u>, finger, and <u>anus</u> or perianal region)

* Primary lesion (chancre) 

* Typically starts out as a solitary, raised <u>papule</u> (usually on the genitals)

* Evolves into a painless, firm <u>ulcer</u> with indurated borders and smooth base

* Resolves spontaneously within 3–6 weeks, typically without scarring [[4]](/library/FkXgpy)

* Nontender regional <u>lymphadenopathy</u> (e.g., involvement of the <u>inguinal lymph nodes</u> in genital <u>primary syphilis</u>)

### Secondary syphilis




* Disseminated disease due to the systemic spread of the <u>spirochetes</u>, inducing an immunologic reaction

* Begins approx. 2–12 weeks after primary infection and typically lasts 2–6 weeks [[5]](/library/8kXOpy)

* <u>Constitutional symptoms</u>

* Generalized nontender <u>lymphadenopathy</u>

* <u>Fever</u>, fatigue, <u>myalgia</u>, <u>headache</u>

* Polymorphic <u>rash</u>  

* Typically disseminated, nonpruritic macular or <u>papular</u> <u>rash</u>

* Involves trunk and extremities, also the palms and soles

* Reddish-brown or <u>copper</u>-colored

* Heals within 6 months, but may recur

* Condylomata lata

* Broad-based, <u>wart</u>-like, smooth, white <u>papular</u> <u>erosions</u>

* Painless

* Located in the anogenital region, <u>intertriginous</u> folds, and on oral <u>mucosa</u>

* Additional lesions

* Patchy <u>alopecia</u> (moth-eaten <u>alopecia</u>)

* <u>Sore throat</u> (acute syphilitic <u>tonsillitis</u>)

* Special variant of <u>secondary syphilis</u>: malignant syphilis

* Severe clinical course in the setting of underlying <u>immunosuppression</u> (e.g., concurrent <u>HIV infection</u>)

* Multiple <u>necrotic</u> <u>ulcerations</u>





> [!NOTE]
> Remember that Secondary Syphilis causes Systemic Symptoms.

### Latent syphilis




* No clinical symptoms, despite seropositivity

* May last months, years, or even for the entire life of the patient

* Disease may resolve, reactivate, or progress to <u>tertiary syphilis</u>

* Early latent: acquired within the last year

* Late latent: acquired > 1 year ago





### Tertiary syphilis




![Tertiary syphilis fact sheet](media/klw3oydyakevs4mf51t8iq2a.jpg)

Tertiary syphilis fact sheet




#### Gumma




* Chronic, destructive granulomatous lesions with a <u>necrotic</u> center that tend to ulcerate

* May affect any organ, e.g., <u>skin</u>, internal organs, bones





![Facial gummas in tertiary syphilis](media/n0x3lprcaux5qtbsj8nc4aks.jpg)

Facial gummas in tertiary syphilis




#### Cardiovascular syphilis




* <u>Aortitis</u>, ascending <u>aortic aneurysm</u> (<u>thoracic aortic aneurysm</u>), syphilitic mesaortitis, <u>aortic root dilation</u> and insufficiency

* Due to <u>Treponema</u>-induced <u>vasculitis</u> of the <u>vasa vasorum</u> of the large vessels (especially the aorta), resulting in vessel wall <u>atrophy</u>, and thereby, <u>aneurysm</u> formation

---

## Subtypes and variants

### Neurosyphilis [[6]](/library/2NcT010)[[7]](/library/lD1veQ0)




* Definition: <u>Neurosyphilis</u> is an infection with treponemal invasion of the <u>CNS</u> (e.g., <u>meninges</u>, <u>cerebral vasculature</u> and/or <u>parenchyma</u>). The diagnosis is based on characteristic clinical features in conjunction with supportive <u>CSF</u> findings.

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: can occur at any stage of infection

* ∼ 0.8 % of infected individuals with early syphilis  [[8]](/library/RbWltP0)

* More common in states of <u>immunosuppression</u> (e.g., <u>coinfection</u> with <u>HIV</u>)

* Clinical features: highly variable

* Acute syphilitic meningitis (e.g., neck stiffness, <u>nausea</u>)

* Subacute <u>stroke</u>, <u>meningitis</u>, and/or <u>cranial nerve disorders</u>

* Paretic neurosyphilis: chronic, progressive <u>meningoencephalitis</u>, resulting in widespread <u>cerebral atrophy</u> and <u>major neurocognitive disorder</u>

* Early manifestations include <u>personality</u> changes and deficits of <u>memory</u> and judgment.

* Can cause neurologic symptoms, including <u>dysarthria</u>, <u>hypotonia</u>, and <u>tremors</u>

* Argyll Robertson pupil  

* Bilateral <u>miosis</u>

* <u>Pupils</u> accommodate but do not react to direct or indirect light.

* Tabes dorsalis (<u>syphilitic myelopathy</u>): <u>demyelination</u> of the <u>dorsal columns</u> and the <u>dorsal root ganglia</u>

* Impaired <u>proprioception</u> → progressive sensory broad-based <u>ataxia</u> (<u>Romberg test</u> is positive)

* Absent <u>deep tendon reflexes</u>

* <u>Dysesthesias</u>

* Loss of sensation, predominantly in the lower extremities

* Sharp, shooting <u>pain</u> in the legs and the abdomen

* <u>Charcot joint</u>

* Diagnostics: <u>CSF</u> studies must be interpreted in the clinical context. Supportive findings are listed.

* Reactive;  <u>Venereal Disease Research Laboratory</u> test (<u>VDRL</u>)

* <u>Lymphocytic</u> <u>pleocytosis</u>

* <u>HIV</u> negative: <u>WBCs</u> > 5/mmÂ³

* <u>HIV</u> positive: <u>WBCs</u> > 20/mm³

* Elevated protein

* Positive <u>fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption test</u>

* Treatment: <u>penicillin</u>; See “<u>Treatment of syphilis</u>” for details.





> [!TIP]
> Patients with syphilis but without <u>neurosyphilis</u> can have unexplained <u>CSF</u> abnormalities. In patients with clinical features of <u>neurosyphilis</u>, a reactive <u>CSF</u>-<u>VDRL</u> strongly supports the diagnosis. [[6]](/library/2NcT010)




![Argyll-Robertson pupil](media/n46xg7iqpnt6t4u7ajbb3166.jpg)

Argyll-Robertson pupil




### Other [[6]](/library/2NcT010)




* Otosyphilis: infection affecting the cochleovestibular system

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: can occur at any stage of infection

* Clinical features: <u>tinnitus</u>, <u>vertigo</u>, and/or <u>sensorineural hearing loss</u> (unilateral or bilateral)

* Ocular syphilis: infection affecting the <u>eye</u> 

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: can occur at any stage of infection

* Clinical features: <u>eye pain</u> or redness, <u>floaters</u>, light <u>sensitivity</u>, blurry <u>vision</u>, and/or permanent <u>vision loss</u>

* <u>Syphilis during pregnancy</u>: See “<u>Congenital syphilis</u>.”

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach




* Perform a focused clinical evaluation that includes exposure history.

* If lesions are present, order direct detection.

* Order both <u>nontreponemal tests</u> and <u>treponemal tests</u> for:

* Patients with <u>clinical features of syphilis</u>

* Patients who meet the criteria for <u>screening for syphilis</u>.

* Consider additional studies (e.g., <u>lumbar puncture</u>) based on the clinical assessment.





### Clinical evaluation [[6]](/library/2NcT010)




* All patients

* Exposure history and any prior syphilis diagnoses

* Examination of <u>skin</u> and <u>mucosal</u> surfaces (e.g., <u>oral cavity</u>, <u>rectum</u>, <u>vagina</u>, <u>cervix</u>)

* Patients with visual or <u>hearing</u> symptoms

* Focused sensory assessment (e.g., <u>visual acuity</u>, <u>focused hearing exam</u>)

* <u>Cranial nerve</u> exam

* Patients with neurological deficits : complete <u>neurological examination</u>





> [!TIP]
> A detailed assessment of exposure history is essential for distinguishing early <u>latent syphilis</u> (infected ≤ 1 year) versus late <u>latent syphilis</u> (infected > 1 year) in asymptomatic seropositive patients. [[6]](/library/2NcT010)




### Direct detection [[9]](/library/8w1OkQ0)




* Indication: the presence of a <u>rash</u> or lesions consistent with syphilis, e.g., <u>exudative</u> <u>chancre</u>, <u>condyloma</u> [[6]](/library/2NcT010)

* Methods: Detection requires specialized laboratory equipment since <u>T. pallidum</u> cannot be cultivated in vitro or visualized with <u>light microscopy</u>. [[10]](/library/N91-nQ0)

* <u>Darkfield microscopy</u>: visualization of motile <u>spirochetes</u> on <u>wet mount</u> under a dark-field microscope  [[9]](/library/8w1OkQ0)

* Direct fluorescent <u>antibody</u> for <u>T. pallidum</u>: visualization of immunofluorescent <u>antibodies</u> on the specimen

* <u>Nucleic acid amplification</u> (e.g., <u>PCR</u>)

* Immunohistopathology

* <u>Accuracy</u>: <u>gold standard</u> to detect primary and <u>secondary syphilis</u>; high <u>specificity</u> but nonsensitive





### <u>Serological studies</u>  [[6]](/library/2NcT010)[[7]](/library/lD1veQ0)[[11]](/library/Sjby-t)




* Serological studies for syphilis can miss early <u>primary syphilis</u>, as <u>antibodies</u> do not develop until 1–4 weeks after lesions appear. [[11]](/library/Sjby-t)

* <u>Syphilis testing algorithms</u>, which combine nontreponemal and <u>treponemal tests</u>, are used to confirm a diagnosis.

* When interpreting results:

* Consider clinical context (i.e., clinical features, <u>risk factors</u>, treatment history)

* Be aware that <u>serologic testing</u> may remain positive in patients previously treated for syphilis.

* Consider consulting an infectious disease specialist for assistance.





#### Nontreponemal tests (NTT) [[6]](/library/2NcT010)[[9]](/library/8w1OkQ0)




* Indications

* Initial screening

* Monitoring response to treatment, i.e., with <u>titer</u> level

* Assessing for syphilis reinfection [[6]](/library/2NcT010)

* Mechanism: quantitative detection of <u>antibodies</u> against lipoidal <u>antigens</u>, e.g., <u>cardiolipin</u>

* Types: both have comparable performance, are widely available, and cost-efficient

* Rapid plasma reagin (<u>RPR</u>): most commonly used test

* Venereal Disease Research Laboratory test (<u>VDRL</u>): often used in the evaluation of <u>cerebrospinal fluid</u> for <u>neurosyphilis</u>  [[12]](/library/tD1XTQ0)

* <u>Accuracy</u>: highly sensitive but nonspecific; positive in ∼ 62–78% of patients with <u>primary syphilis</u> [[12]](/library/tD1XTQ0)

* False-negative NTT:

* Early <u>primary syphilis</u>

* <u>Prozone phenomenon</u>

* Longstanding untreated syphilis with seroreversion

* False-positive NTT: due to cross-reacting <u>antibodies</u> [[11]](/library/Sjby-t)[[12]](/library/tD1XTQ0)

* Autoimmune (e.g., <u>systemic lupus erythematosus</u>, <u>rheumatoid arthritis</u>)

* Infections (e.g., <u>malaria</u>, <u>leprosy</u>, <u>Epstein-Barr virus</u>, viral <u>hepatitis</u>)

* <u>Rheumatic fever</u> [[13]](/library/fw1kRQ0)

* <u>Pregnancy</u>

* Prescription drugs (e.g., <u>chlorpromazine</u>, <u>procainamide</u>)  [[14]](/library/rx1fBQ0)

* <u>Intravenous drug use</u>

* Important considerations

* After infection, NTT <u>titers</u> can undergo seroreversion and convert to negative even if syphilis is not treated.

* After treatment, NTT <u>titers</u> can remain elevated despite successful treatment (serofast state).





> [!NOTE]
> False-Positive results on <u>VDRL</u> with Pregnancy, Viral infection (e.g., <u>EBV</u>, <u>hepatitis</u>), Drugs (e.g., <u>chlorpromazine</u>, <u>procainamide</u>), Rheumatic <u>fever</u> (rare), Lupus, and Leprosy




#### Treponemal tests (TT) [[9]](/library/8w1OkQ0)[[11]](/library/Sjby-t)




* Indications

* Initial screening

* <u>Confirmatory test</u> in the standard testing algorithm

* Mechanism: : qualitative detection of <u>antibodies</u> to treponemal <u>antigens</u>

* Types: Many TTs exist; examples of common types are listed here.

* Fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption test (<u>FTA-ABS</u>)

* Treponema pallidum particle agglutination (<u>TPPA</u>)

* <u>IgG</u>/<u>IgM</u> immunoassay (enzyme or chemiluminescence)

* <u>Accuracy</u>

* New infection: high <u>sensitivity</u> and <u>specificity</u>

* False-negative TT: early <u>primary syphilis</u>

* False-positive TT: inflammatory diseases (e.g., <u>SLE</u>); infections (e.g., <u>Lyme disease</u>) [[15]](/library/291T5Q0)

* Reinfection: limited <u>sensitivity</u> and <u>specificity</u>  [[16]](/library/qw1CPQ0)

* Important considerations: After infection, TT <u>titer</u> typically stays positive indefinitely.





#### Syphilis testing algorithms [[6]](/library/2NcT010)[[11]](/library/Sjby-t)




##### Overview of syphilis testing algorithms [[6]](/library/2NcT010)[[11]](/library/Sjby-t)




* Either the standard algorithm or reverse algorithm can be used to diagnose syphilis.

* If the initial test is positive, both algorithms require an additional test to confirm the diagnosis.

* Both tests positive: A current or past infection is likely.

* Previously treated: Consider possible reinfection, treatment failure, or a <u>serofast state</u>; see “<u>Posttreatment assessment for syphilis</u>.”

* No previous treatment: active syphilis infection highly likely

* Second test negative: Next steps vary based on the testing algorithm used.

* If the initial test in either algorithm is negative

* Low-risk patients: Syphilis is unlikely; no further testing is necessary.

* High-risk patients 

* Early <u>primary syphilis</u> cannot be excluded.

* Offer presumptive treatment; if declined, repeat testing.





![Syphilis serological testing algorithm](media/blff7j9l9wcgbybu8cidccrm.jpg)

Syphilis serological testing algorithm




##### Standard algorithm [[6]](/library/2NcT010)[[11]](/library/Sjby-t)




* Initial test: NTT

* Positive NTT: Perform a TT.

* Negative NTT: Further management depends on risk status; see “<u>Overview of syphilis testing algorithms</u>.”

* Second test: TT

* Positive TT: Current or past syphilis infection is likely; see “<u>Overview of syphilis testing algorithms</u>.”

* Negative TT

* <u>False-positive NTT</u> likely

* If <u>risk factors</u> are present, repeat after 2–4 weeks or, if follow-up is unlikely, consider treating.





##### Reverse algorithm [[6]](/library/2NcT010)[[11]](/library/Sjby-t)




* Initial test: TT

* Positive TT: Perform an NTT.

* Negative TT: Further management depends on risk status; see “<u>Overview of syphilis testing algorithms</u>.”

* Second test: NTT

* Positive NTT: current syphilis infection or <u>serofast state</u>; see “<u>Overview of syphilis testing algorithms</u>”

* Negative NTT: Perform a different TT. 

* Positive second TT: Current or past infection is likely; see “<u>Overview of syphilis testing algorithms</u>.”

* Negative second TT

* <u>False-positive TT</u> likely

* If <u>risk factors</u> are present, repeat after 2–4 weeks or, if follow-up is unlikely, consider treating.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Serologic tests</u> may be negative in early syphilis. If there is high clinical suspicion, offer presumptive treatment. Alternatively, if a suitable lesion exists, order a direct <u>pathogen</u> test (e.g., <u>darkfield microscopy</u>, <u>PCR</u>) to establish the diagnosis. [[7]](/library/lD1veQ0)[[11]](/library/Sjby-t)[[17]](/library/ew1x3Q0)




### Additional studies [[6]](/library/2NcT010)




After confirming syphilis infection, order the following studies based on the clinical scenario.




* All patients: <u>screening for sexually transmitted infections</u> (e.g., <u>HIV</u>, <u>gonorrhea</u>, <u>chlamydia</u>)

* Patients of childbearing age: <u>pregnancy test</u>

* Suspected <u>neurosyphilis</u>

* <u>Lumbar puncture</u> prior to initiating treatment

* See “Subtypes and variants” for details on interpreting <u>CSF</u> studies. [[6]](/library/2NcT010)[[7]](/library/lD1veQ0)

* Suspected <u>ocular syphilis</u> or <u>otosyphilis</u>: functional sensory testing (e.g., <u>audiogram</u>, <u>slit lamp examination</u>)





> [!TIP]
> No single finding can establish a diagnosis of <u>neurosyphilis</u>, <u>ocular syphilis</u>, or <u>otosyphilis</u>. These diagnoses can occur at any stage of infection and, if suspected, require prompt evaluation by a specialist. [[6]](/library/2NcT010)




#### Imaging [[18]](/library/uw1pkQ0)




* Indication: concern for <u>cardiovascular syphilis</u> (e.g., reports of <u>chest pain</u>, <u>dyspnea</u>)

* Modalities

* Initial study: CT or <u>MRI</u> chest with contrast

* If inconclusive: <u>angiography</u>

* Findings [[19]](/library/VnYGHp)

* <u>Aneurysms</u> of the <u>thoracic aorta</u> or <u>aortic arch</u>

* Heavy aortic calcification: may include the aortic root, <u>ascending aorta</u>, <u>aortic arch</u>, and <u>thoracic aorta</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>Intimal</u> calcifications of the aorta may have a tree bark appearance on CT or <u>MRI</u>. [[20]](/library/o910oQ0)

---

## Treatment

### Approach [[6]](/library/2NcT010)




* Initiate <u>antibiotic</u> treatment in patients with:

* Confirmed syphilis infection

* Suspected early infection (prior to <u>seroconversion</u>, history of sexual contact with a person with syphilis)

* Inform patients about the possibility of a <u>Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction</u> to treatment.

* Screen for and treat any <u>coinfections</u> with other <u>STIs</u>. (see “<u>Diagnostics of syphilis</u>”).

* Evaluate and treat sexual partners.

* Initiate presumptive treatment for:

* All sexual partners from the 90 days before diagnosis

* Sexual partners from > 90 days before diagnosis if there is concern for loss to follow-up

* The trace-back period for testing depends on the stage of syphilis.

* <u>Primary syphilis</u>: 3 months before symptoms started

* <u>Secondary syphilis</u>: 6 months before symptoms started

* Early <u>latent syphilis</u>: 12 months before diagnosis

* Advise patients to:

* Abstain from all sexual contact until all of the following criteria are met: [[11]](/library/Sjby-t)

* Symptoms have resolved

* 7 days have passed since the treatment course was completed

* Sexual partners have been treated and meet the above criteria

* Use <u>barrier contraception</u> until treatment response has been confirmed with NTT <u>titers</u>.

* Offer <u>counseling on STI prevention</u>, including <u>HIV PrEP</u> if appropriate. [[6]](/library/2NcT010)

* Consult infectious diseases for complex cases  and specialists for affected organs (e.g., ophthalmology for <u>ocular syphilis</u>).

* For further information on management in <u>pregnancy</u>, see “<u>Syphilis in pregnancy</u>.”





> [!WARNING]
> Beyond the <u>newborn</u> period, a diagnosis of syphilis in children is highly suspicious for <u>child sexual abuse</u>. [[6]](/library/2NcT010)




> [!TIP]
> All sexual contacts of patients with syphilis should be identified, evaluated, and treated.




### <u>Antibiotic therapy</u> [[6]](/library/2NcT010)




* <u>Penicillin G</u> is the first-line therapy for all patients.

* Patients with confirmed <u>penicillin</u> <u>allergy</u> 

* For patients with <u>neurosyphilis</u>; , <u>ocular syphilis</u>, <u>otosyphilis</u>, and/or during <u>pregnancy</u>, initiate <u>allergen desensitization</u> and treat with <u>penicillin</u>.

* For all other patients, consider, e.g., <u>doxycycline</u> or <u>ceftriaxone</u>.

| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Stage or subtype |  | <u>Penicillin</u> regimens (first-line) | Alternative regimens (if nonpregnant) |
| <br>Primary, secondary, or early <u>latent syphilis</u> <br> |  | <br>* <u>Penicillin G</u> given as a single dose DOSAGE [[6]](/library/2NcT010)<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Doxycycline</u> for 14 days DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Ceftriaxone</u> for 10 days (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE<br><br><br> |
| <br>Tertiary or late <u>latent syphilis</u> <br> |  | <br>* <u>Penicillin G</u> for 3 weeks DOSAGE [[6]](/library/2NcT010)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Doxycycline</u> for 4 weeks DOSAGE<br><br> |
| <u>Neurosyphilis</u>, <u>ocular syphilis</u>, or <u>otosyphilis</u> |  | <br><br>* Intravenous <u>penicillin G</u> for 10–14 days DOSAGE [[6]](/library/2NcT010)<br><br>* OR intramuscular <u>penicillin G</u> for 10–14 days DOSAGE PLUS <u>probenecid</u> for 10–14 days DOSAGE if IV therapy is not preferred and adherence can be ensured [[6]](/library/2NcT010)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Preferred: Refer for <u>penicillin</u> <u>allergen desensitization</u>.<br><br>* Alternative: <u>Ceftriaxone</u> DOSAGE for 10–14 days may be considered (<u>off-label</u>).<br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> If <u>neurosyphilis</u> is suspected, perform a <u>lumbar puncture</u> and <u>CSF analysis</u> before starting treatment.




### Posttreatment assessment for syphilis [[6]](/library/2NcT010)




* Perform a clinical evaluation and measure NTT <u>titers</u> at:

* Nonpregnant patients: 6 and 12 months after treatment  [[6]](/library/2NcT010)

* Pregnant patients: depends on <u>gestation</u>, see “<u>Syphilis in pregnancy</u>.”

* Compare NTT <u>titers</u> to pretreatment results.

* NTT <u>titer</u> decreased by ≥ fourfold: successful treatment response

* NTT <u>titer</u> increased by ≥ fourfold: treatment failure or reinfection

* NTT <u>titer</u> unchanged or changed by < fourfold within 12 months: <u>serofast state</u> or treatment failure

* If NTT <u>titers</u> have not decreased by ≥ fourfold, determine whether this is due to a <u>serofast state</u>, reinfection, or treatment failure.

* Factors suggestive of a <u>serofast state</u>

* <u>Neurosyphilis</u>

* Older age

* Later stage syphilis

* Low <u>titers</u> (< 1:8)

* Recurrent treated infections

* Factors suggestive of reinfection or treatment failure

* A fourfold increase in <u>titers</u> for > 2 weeks

* Persistent or recurrent symptoms

* Consult a specialist if the diagnosis is uncertain.

* If a <u>serofast state</u> is suspected:

* Assess for <u>HIV</u>.

* Perform additional <u>neurological examinations</u>.

* Reassess clinically every year and perform <u>serology</u>.

* If there is concern for loss to follow-up, re-treat.

* If reinfection or treatment failure is suspected: Re-treat patients with weekly IM <u>penicillin G</u> for 3 weeks (see “<u>Antibiotic therapy for syphilis infection</u>”).





> [!WARNING]
> Either type of NTT (i.e., <u>RPR</u> or <u>VDRL</u>) may be used to assess treatment response, but do not compare across types when assessing the trend in <u>titers</u>. For example, a <u>titer</u> for <u>RPR</u> can only be compared to prior <u>titers</u> of <u>RPR</u>.

---

## Complications

* Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction: acute, transient, systemic reaction to bacterial <u>endotoxin</u>-like substances and pyrogens that are released after initiation of <u>antibiotic therapy</u> ;  [[21]](/library/aSaQyP)[[22]](/library/STYyJo)[[23]](/library/hTYcqo)

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* Commonly seen during treatment of infections with <u>spirochetes</u> (<u>Borrelia</u>, <u>Leptospira</u>)

* In syphilis, the <u>Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction</u> is most often seen if treatment begins in the early phases of the secondary stage.

* Clinical features

* <u>Flu-like symptoms</u>: <u>fever</u>, chills, <u>headache</u>, <u>myalgia</u>

* Accompanied by <u>tachypnea</u>, <u>hypotension</u>, and <u>tachycardia</u>

* Syphilitic exanthema may flare up

* Usually <u>self-limiting</u> within 12–24 hours

* Treatment

* <u>NSAIDs</u> for symptomatic treatment

* May consider meptazinol

* <u>Chorioretinitis</u> [[24]](/library/wkXhJy)




We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.
